text: I am checking whether Q supplies a transferable failure mechanism for P, especially whether P’s pairwise comparison noise is independent enough for rank aggregation under changing participation. I will separate evidence for comparative decisions from conjectures about LMM judging.

I am checking whether Q offers a specific mechanism that violates an assumption in P, beyond generic LMM judge noise. I will inspect P’s estimator and dynamic-participation claim against Q’s actual evidence before proposing an experiment.

The scan overstates transfer: Q studies LLM traders, not LMM judges. Q §4 reports quote anchoring and role asymmetry, and §5 reports urgency/execution words associated with trade crossing only for Gemini Large; the authors explicitly say traces are suggestive, noncausal, and not generalizable. P §Method compares only two active agents’ egocentric images with fixed task prompt, uses both orders to mitigate position bias, and §Theory proves recovery of an LMM latent Bradley–Terry preference, not true contribution. Thus Q cannot establish P comparator failure; it motivates a targeted test of systematic context-conditioned preference drift that extra comparisons cannot average away.

The abstract-level urgency transfer is weak: Q §Analysis of Reasoning (inputs/Q.tex:404–438) analyzes Gemini trader decisions, only one exposed trace model, and says lexical shifts are suggestive, not causal. P §Method (inputs/P.tex:294–333) uses an LMM referee on two egocentric images, a different role. The more testable overlap is structured context bias: Q §Individual Behavior (Q:398–403) reports opposing-side agents anchor to the first offer even without a mechanical constraint; P:201–205 claims pairwise comparison accommodates changing active counts, and P:294–299 says ordered comparisons mitigate position bias. This motivates testing roster/context sensitivity beyond left-right order, but Q does not establish it occurs in P.

Sharper P-specific test: MARS-Bench displays each agent’s battery level in the image (P Fig. 3 caption, around P:419), and depletion removes/re-enters agents (P:427). Q §5 associates urgency language with a switch in traders’ actions (Q:404–441). Hypothesis only: an LMM referee may use battery/impending exit as an urgency shortcut when judging who *made* greater contribution, so its pairwise preference can be systematically wrong exactly near roster transitions. Audit identical archived image pairs with only rendered battery icon or noncausal urgency cue altered, both image orders, while simulator state/dense-reward label is fixed. Stratify real comparisons by battery and join/exit proximity; test whether cue shifts judgments, accuracy, and downstream shaped credits. This is more specific than generic LMM noise, but no current evidence it occurs.

Sharper question: in P’s changing-active-set episodes, does extra querying denoise comparisons or make a stable, wrong context heuristic more confident? Q supplies the *possibility* of structured heuristic behavior (opening-offer anchoring despite no constraint, Q:398–403; urgency-associated crossing in one model, Q:404–438), not evidence about referees. P’s proposition (P:361–388) only converges to the LMM latent Bradley–Terry preference, while P:550–552 reports pooled pairwise accuracy and improved success with more queries, and P:521 reports 3-cycle/NLL without transition stratification. Test frozen MARS-Bench states immediately before/after battery removal or respawn (P:435), stratify dense-reward label error, rank error, pair cycles, and policy success by active-set transition; vary independent repeated queries and inject controlled persistent salience/urgency bias. Distinguish variance reduction from bias: under a fixed wrong pair preference, more comparisons converge to wrong credit. Q’s CoT lexical statistic is optional exploratory evidence, not a causal diagnostic.

Formal reason the test matters: if true step contribution is \(v_i\) but comparator follows \(\Pr(i\succ j)=\sigma[(v_i-v_j)+\beta(u_i-u_j)]\), with \(u\) an urgency/battery cue, the data are exactly Bradley–Terry with latent score \(v_i+\beta u_i\). Rank aggregation can have zero 3-cycles and a good held-out fit, yet as queries \(K\) increase it converges more confidently to the biased score. If roster changes also change \(u\), the score drifts at the exact condition where P claims robustness. P §Theory (P:361–389) only guarantees latent LMM preference recovery and explicitly limits its Shapley reading; P reports 8.95% 3-cycles and 0.41 NLL (P:~510), neither tests calibration to true contribution. This is a model counterexample, not empirical evidence of an actual battery bias.

Caveat to the battery-icon intervention (#5): P:430–436 and P:665 make battery causally relevant to future participation, so holding simulator state/dense reward fixed while repainting the icon creates an inconsistent observation; a judgment shift would show cue sensitivity, not necessarily an error in true contribution. Better primary estimand is conditional *real-state* pairwise error near depletion/respawn against P’s dense reward proxy (P:1072), plus simulator counterfactual marginal contribution if feasible. Use icon edits only as a mechanism probe, compare an irrelevant matched visual cue and state explicitly that per-step dense reward is an imperfect credit oracle.

Corrections to #5/#7: P battery icon is at P:397 (Fig. 3 caption), not ~419; P cycle/NLL numbers are at P:521. An exact finite-parameter Bradley–Terry *probability* model can generate observed 3-cycles by sampling, so “zero 3-cycles” was too strong. The valid claim is that its latent ordering is transitive and can fit held-out comparison probabilities well while remaining systematically misaligned with true contribution.

Ada #8 is right: battery controls future participation, so repainting it while freezing the simulator is an inconsistent-observation *mechanism probe*, not a valid estimate of credit error. Primary experiment should use real archived states and compare pairwise label error versus P’s per-agent dense reward proxy (P:1072), stratified by distance to depletion/respawn and controlled for task, score gap, visibility, agent identity, and progress. A simulator counterfactual marginal-contribution measure would strengthen the target because dense reward is itself only a proxy. If battery edits flip judgments, report cue sensitivity separately; only a mismatch with a defensible contribution target supports failure.

Further check on mechanism: Q’s market also loses participants during a round after each trade (Q:235–247), but Q does not identify active-count change as the cause of urgency/anchoring; do not import that causal claim. P’s comparison input is two images plus task prompt (P:294–317), so changing a *third* agent’s roster status need not change a frozen pair’s LMM output unless that status appears in the images/prompt. The defensible test targets visible battery/teammate context and aggregation under real entry/exit states. P’s potential is softmax over active scores (P:338–353), so active-set changes can alter potentials mechanically; this alone is not evidence of incorrect credit or policy-invariance failure.

Best account: ask whether *structured, transition-linked comparator bias*, rather than random noise, survives P’s rank aggregation and harms finite-training credit near agent removal/re-entry. Q’s strongest transferable result is context-sensitive action behavior (unconstrained opposite-side anchoring, Q:398–403), with urgency words only suggestive in one trader model (Q:404–441). P:285–303 uses only a pair’s images and fixed prompt, so roster size itself is not directly shown to the referee; effects must pass through changed visible scene/battery cues or through aggregation/softmax over a changed active set. P:361–389 guarantees recovery of the referee’s latent preference under Bradley–Terry, not contribution truth; P:521 3-cycle/NLL and P:550–552 pooled accuracy/query gains do not isolate transition-local systematic bias. Feasible study: save real 2–4-agent MARS-Bench states, get repeated ordered judgments, evaluate conditional error against dense reward (P:1072) and, if possible, simulator counterfactual credit; estimate bias/variance across distance to roster change and query count; compare performance with transition-targeted cue correction versus random-noise-matched control. A positive conditional error that persists/increases with queries and changes learned success could support publication. Null transition effect or no downstream difference would defeat the specific Q–P connection. This is a sharpened hypothesis, not an established result.

Proposed publication test: archive real MARS-Bench trajectories, prespecify windows around actual battery exit/respawn, and compare the same LMM’s pair labels with P’s dense-reward proxy in those windows versus matched stable-roster states (match task, reward gap, visibility, progress, identity). Estimate whether extra *independent* calls reduce error or merely sharpen wrong margins; report Bradley–Terry fit/cycles as diagnostics, since good fit does not imply contribution calibration. Then train with transition-aware reliability weighting or withholding of low-confidence credits and compare held-out team success against original MARS-RA at matched query budget. Battery-icon edits are secondary cue probes only. This would be publication-worthy only if a reproducible transition-specific bias and downstream cost appear; absent that, Q is a motivation rather than a substantive connexion. P’s current pooled accuracies (P:550–552, 1030–1074), cycle/NLL (P:521), and limitations (P:642) partly cover generic judge unreliability, so a generic audit alone is not enough.

A useful discriminant beyond the transition-stratified audit: P:285–303 sends only simultaneous egocentric images and a task prompt, yet asks which agent *made* the greater contribution; no action history is specified. Since battery depletes through actions and triggers removal (P:427), near-transition dense-reward error could reflect missing evidence rather than a salience/urgency heuristic. In archived real states, pair standard image-only judgments with otherwise identical judgments that also receive a short verified action/outcome history, and evaluate both against the same per-agent dense-reward proxy (P:1072), matched for score gap and visibility. If added history closes a transition-specific error gap, information loss is implicated; if error persists but controlled battery-cue masking changes the choice, cue reliance becomes more plausible. Neither contrast alone establishes causal credit truth. Q:397–403 supports context sensitivity through unconstrained opening-offer anchoring; Q:405–442 urgency terms are suggestive, not causal, so the lexical analysis should stay secondary.

Refinement to #14/#16: P asks the referee which agent "made a greater contribution" from simultaneous image pairs and task prompt (P:285–303), while its accuracy label is agreement with per-agent step-wise dense progress rewards (P:665, 1072). Near battery exit (P:397, 427), current progress, past action contribution, and future ability to help can diverge. Prespecify the estimand: use the dense reward only as P’s own immediate-progress proxy, and if testing actual credit, estimate a simulator counterfactual effect on downstream team return under matched rollouts. A transition-local disagreement with dense reward alone cannot establish that the referee is wrong. For #16, add only verified prior action/outcome history available at decision time, with an equal-information-control prompt and no dense-reward/hidden-state label leakage; compare its transition-specific accuracy change against matched stable-roster states. This distinguishes an image information bottleneck from cue reliance better, though it still does not prove Q’s urgency mechanism.
